L29: In this letter, a reliable, simple, and intuitive approach for hyperspectral imagery (HSI) anomaly detection (AD) is presented. This method, namely, the global iterative principal component analysis (PCA) reconstruction-error-based anomaly detector (GIPREBAD), examines AD by computing errors (residuals) associated with reconstructing the original image using PCA projections.
L30: PCA is a linear transformation and feature extraction process commonly used in HSI and frequently appears in operation prior to any AD task. PCA features represent a projection of the original data into lower-dimensional subspace. An iterative approach is used to mitigate outlier influence on background covariance estimates. GIPREBAD results are provided using receiver-operating-characteristic curves for HSI from the hyperspectral digital imagery collection experiment.
L31: Results are compared against the Reed-Xiaoli (RX) algorithm, the linear RX (LRX) algorithm, and the support vector data description (SVDD) algorithm. The results show that the proposed GIPREBAD method performs favorably compared with RX, LRX, and SVDD and is both intuitively and computationally simpler than either RX or SVDD.

L105: I. I NTRODUCTION
L106: 
L107: H YPERSPECTRAL imaging (HSI) systems collect both
L108: 
L109: spatial and spectral features and perform imaging spec-
L110: 
L111: troscopy [1]. HSI differs from multispectral imaging by collect-
L112: 
L113: ing ﬁnely sampled, as opposed to coarsely sampled, spectral
L114: 
L115: bands [1]. The ﬁne spectral sampling of HSI permits the
L116: remote detection, examination, and identiﬁcation of materials
L117: 
L118: by analyzing differences in both spectral and spatial charac-
L119: 
L120: teristics. HSI is therefore used in three primary applications:
L121: 
L122: anomaly detection (AD), change detection, and spectral signa-
L123: 
L124: ture matching [1]. HSI AD is considered as the detection of
L125: 
L126: pixels statistically different from the background of the image,
L127: 
L128: with no apriori information about the content of the image [1].
L129: 
L130: Two general philosophies have emerged in HSI AD algorithm
L131: development: 1) highly accurate or tuned, but computation-

L164: Since HSI contains a large amount of data, dimensionality
L165: reduction (DR) is frequently employed for feature selection/
L166: 
L167: extraction. PCA is commonly applied to HSI for DR with
L168: 
L169: further processing by an AD algorithm [1], [10]–[15]. In this
L170: 
L171: research, the DR step and the AD step are consolidated. The
L172: 
L173: reconstruction error (residual analysis) evident in PCA is used
L174: 
L175: to identify potential anomalies. The general philosophy follows
L176: 
L177: that a reconstruction error may be obtained from a DR by
L178: 
L179: reprojecting retained features into the data’s original space.
L180: Naturally, since these projections are biased by the majority
L181: 
L182: class (considered as the background of an image), reconstruct-
L183: 
L184: ing the original data using the projections should yield poor
L185: 
L186: reconstructions for anomalies. By a simple extension of this
L187: 
L188: logic, such poorly reconstructed points are labeled as anoma-
L189: 
L190: lies. Reconstruction errors for AD, therefore, achieve AD as a
L191: 
L192: byproduct of data compression.
L193: 
L194: Image reconstruction has been considered for HSI noise
L195: reduction [16], and reconstruction errors have been considered
L196: 
L197: in prior works for outlier detection, c.f. [17]–[19], compressive
L198: 
L199: sensing [20], signal reconstruction [21], and replicator neural
L200: 
L201: networks [22]; however, none of these applications were for
L202: 
L203: remote sensing AD. Fowler and Du [23] considered the re-
L204: 
L205: construction error for signal recovery in HSI; however, they
L206: 
L207: employed a separate AD step to segment background and
L208: 
L209: anomalies into separate bins. Similar to the method presented
L210: herein, Li and Du [24] presented an HSI reconstructive error
L211: 
L212: AD; however, it was based on a window approach. Gao et al.
L213: 
L214: [25] considered PCA as a second step for DR in compressive
L215: 
L216: sensing. In [3], manifold reconstructive errors were used to ﬁnd
L217: 
L218: regions of possible anomalies with Mahalanobis distance used
L219: 
L220: to discriminate points.
L221: 
L222: Herein, the authors suggest methods to create a PCA re-
L223: 
L224: constructive error AD that 1) uses PCA reconstructive error
L225: as a measure in AD; 2) employs adaptive noise ﬁltering it-
L226: 
L227: eratively to reﬁne the solution [7]; and 3) uses zero-bin his-
L228: 
L229: tograms (ZBHs) [26] to select anomalies from a set of scores.

L232: 
L233: reconstruction-error-based anomaly detector (GIPREBAD) for

L292: B. PCA and HSI
L293: 
L294: HSI data are reorganized into a matrix form for processing by
L295: 
L296: PCA. Although some disagreement exists on the applicability
L297: 
L298: and appropriateness of PCA for HSI [28], PCA is a commonly
L299: 
L300: used tool because it is simple to use and offers reasonable re-
L301: sults [1]. Additionally, from an information theory perspective,
L302: 
L303: PCA is the most efﬁcient method of DR due to its accounting
L304: 
L305: for the most variance in a data set with the least number of
L306: 
L307: dimensions [29].
L308: 
L309: In general, the ﬁrst PC of a given HSI image is interpreted
L310: 
L311: as broadband intensity variation across the spectra, with subse-
L312: 
L313: quent PCs providing primary global spectral differences across
L314: 
L315: the image [1]. Eismann [1] considers that rare features or
L316: anomalies often dominate trailing components with low vari-
L317: 
L318: ance. Therefore, eliminating or ignoring trailing PCs, as done
L319: 
L320: in many PCA applications [30] including HSI [1], may reduce
L321: 
L322: AD performance. In this letter, PCA reconstruction error is
L323: 
L324: employed, and it can be shown to be a function of the linear sum
L325: 
L326: of the trailing principal components. This way, the GIPREBAD
L327: 
L328: method, espoused herein, accounts for information in the trail-
L329: 
L330: ing principal components and may offer advantages over other
L331: detection algorithms that completely discard this information.
L332: 
L333: Kaiser’s criterion, a method of basic estimation of data
L334: 
L335: dimensionality based on the mean eigenvalue of the correlation
L336: 
L337: matrix [30], was used to assess the overall dimensionality of the
L338: 
L339: data. Kaiser’s criterion speciﬁes the number of retained PCs,
L340: 
L341: i.e., k,withasimplerulethat k is the number of eigenvalues
L342: 
L343: greater than the mean eigenvalue [30]. Kaiser’s criterion offers
L344: 
L345: reasonable performance for hyperspectral digital imagery col-
L346: lection experiment (HYDICE) imagery, as seen in [31], and is
L347: 
L348: a simple method to implement.

L613: V. C ONCLUSION
L614: 
L615: Herein, a simple, intuitive, efﬁcient, and effective algo-
L616: 
L617: rithm, namely, GIPREBAD, for HSI AD has been presented.
L618: 
L619: GIPREBAD leverages PCA feature extraction for both DR and
L620: 
L621: AD. GIPREBAD results also compared favorably with RX,
L622: LRX, and SVDD in detection performance and showed a sig-
L623: 
L624: niﬁcant improvement in computational time. Additionally, on
L625: 
L626: the presented images, GIPREBAD consistently outperformed
L627: 
L628: RX and LRX. Due to GIPREBAD using commonly used HSI
L629: 
L630: tools within a straightforward process, it would be easy to
L631: 
L632: implement GIPREBAD in many HSI applications. GIPREBAD
L633: 
L634: could also potentially see use in real-time compressive sensing
